title: Last week handed me two perfect trading stories. I’m not building anything on either of them.
author: Ok_Map5721
selftext: Last week was a lot. Nov 5: Nasdaq down about 5.5%, chip stocks down around 12%, BTC down 5 to 6%. Roughly $1.1B in crypto liquidations, almost 90% of it longs, and more than half of that in the first hour after the US open. Everyone online had the takeaway ready within hours: crypto now trades like a leveraged Nasdaq, so watch the US open and ride the move. Then Nvidia. Sunday the news about the board probe of the CEO breaks. Monday the stock is down 8% intraday. Tuesday another 5.5%, while AMD and Broadcom actually go up. Thursday he resigns and it opens down around 13%. Another ready-made lesson: big scandal, short it, buy the competitors. Both stories are great. Both are exactly one event. And I've burned enough time on this to know that a fresh story is the most dangerous starting point for a strategy, because it feels like evidence when it's really n = 1. What I do now before I let a story anywhere near a backtest: 1. Count how often it actually happens. Days like Nov 5 come maybe 3 or 4 times a year. Ten years of data gives you a few dozen. Before testing anything I work out how big the effect would need to be for a test that size to even see it. A lot of ideas die right there, before any data, and honestly that's the cheapest place for them to die. 2. Write the rule before looking. If I define "big down day" after watching Nov 5, I'll pick the threshold that makes Nov 5 look perfect without even noticing. Fixed rules first, and every variant I try counts as another attempt. 3. Make sure the event definition doesn't peek. Someone here posted a great example this week: their news filter only counted a jump if price was still far away a few minutes later. t-stat 10. Fixed so it only used data up to the entry, it dropped to about 1.5. My check now: cut the data at the entry time and see if the filter gives the same answer. If it changes, it's using the future. 4. Compare against random. "Shorting after big red days made money" means nothing in a falling market, random shorts made money too. The question is whether the rule beats random entries on the same days with the same holding time. 5. Ask why it would keep working. Who is on the other side, and why can't they stop doing it? If I can't answer that, I don't trust a nice number either. Two things I closed recently that also started as nice stories: a month-end stock/bond rebalancing effect that looked great over 20+ years and fell apart on history it hadn't seen, and rotating small coins by funding rate, about 5 bp a day gross against about 14 bp a day in costs. Both made total sense when I first read about them. Not saying markets are random or that nothing works. Just that a week like this is when it's easiest to fool yourself. How do you all stop yourselves from building on the event of the week?

comments.author: real_PommesPanzer
comments.body: My in development trading not threw this one up as negative news (with huge impact) right when it came up. I directly shorted nvidia because of the spy thing. Best decision so far.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body: nice call, congrats. genuinely curious though: how often does your news flag fire with "huge impact", and how did the other calls go? one great trade is exactly the trap I was writing about, it feels like proof but it's one data point. if the flag fires 50 times and the shorts beat random entries on the same days, that's something. if it's mostly this one, it might just be a good week.

replies.author: real_PommesPanzer
replies.body: It just run for last 1 month and still "early" stage.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
makes sense, a month is still early for anything. one thing worth doing from now on if you aren't already: log every time the flag fires, including the ones you didn't trade, with the price at the moment it fired. after a few months you can check how the flagged moves did on average versus random times, instead of remembering mostly the big wins.

and if you're up for it, DM me when you've got a few months of results, I'd genuinely like to see how it holds up. happy to run the log through the same checks I use on my own stuff. good luck with it.

comments.author: AoideusWasBanned
comments.body:
Point 1 is the one that hurts the most. I've had ideas die the moment I counted how many times the event actually showed up in the data, and tbh that's a cheap death compared to finding out after weeks of tweaking.

The month-end rebalancing one is interesting though. Did it fall apart on older history or newer?

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
glad point 1 landed, that's exactly how it felt for me too.

the month-end one fell apart on \[older / newer\] history, the part the original study didn't use. worth saying the source itself already showed it flat in 2023-24, so it was looking tired before I even touched it. it's a real mechanism, pension funds and balanced funds do have to rebalance, but my guess is it's become crowded enough that whatever's left is too small to trade after costs.

replies.author: AoideusWasBanned
replies.body:
Haha I think the [older / newer] part slipped through.

But if the source already showed it flat in 2023-24, that kind of answers it anyway. Crowded plus costs is my guess too.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body: ha, caught red-handed. that's what I get for posting my draft without reading it back. honest answer: it failed on the history the original study didn't cover, and the flat 2023-24 stretch in the source was already the warning sign. crowded plus costs, agreed.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Counting how often the event actually happens is a good first filter, since a lot of ideas die right there. One habit that helps is keeping a simple log of every idea you test, with the rule written down before the run, so the number of attempts is on record when you judge the best one. Another is deciding up front which stretch of data stays untouched until the end, and only looking at it once. Cymetica's Backtest Labs has a fee setting and an option to hold out the last part of the history, which supports that second habit.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body: agreed on both. and worth saying neither needs a special tool. a text file with the rule and date written before the run, plus cutting off the last chunk of data in your own loader before anything reads it, does the job for free.

comments.author: Substantial_Air_3170
comments.body: The point about defining the event before examining the results is excellent. It's ridiculously easy to turn a memorable selloff into a strategy that seems obvious afterward. When I look at potential setups for moon, that's the kind of hindsight bias I try to watch for. One dramatic example shouldn't become an entire trading system.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body: exactly, and the annoying part is the hindsight version always looks more convincing than the honest one. what helped me most was writing the definition down with a date before I look at anything, even if it's just a line in a text file. if I catch myself wanting to change it after seeing the results, that's usually the moment I'm about to fool myself.
